title: Philemon

stories.title: 📜 Philemon
summaryBullets: Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, and Timothy our brother, To Philemon our beloved fellow worker, (1:1).
to Apphia our sister, to Archippus our fellow soldier, and to the church that meets at your house: (1:2).
Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. (1:3).
I always thank my God, remembering you in my prayers, (1:4).
because I hear about your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love for all the saints. (1:5).
I pray that your partnership in the faith may become effective as you fully acknowledge every good thing that is ours in Christ. (1:6).
I take great joy and encouragement in your love, because you, brother, have refreshed the hearts of the saints. (1:7).
So although in Christ I am bold enough to order you to do what is proper, (1:8).
I prefer to appeal on the basis of love. For I, Paul, am now aged, and a prisoner of Christ Jesus as well. (1:9).
I appeal to you for my child Onesimus, whose father I became while I was in chains. (1:10).
Formerly he was useless to you, but now he has become useful both to you and to me. (1:11).
I am sending back to you him who is my very heart. (1:12).
I would have liked to keep him with me, so that on your behalf he could minister to me in my chains for the gospel. (1:13).
But I did not want to do anything without your consent, so that your goodness will not be out of compulsion, but by your own free will. (1:14).
For perhaps this is why he was separated from you for a while, so that you might have him back for good — (1:15).
no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother. He is especially beloved to me, but even more so to you, both in person and in the Lord. (1:16).
So if you consider me a partner, receive him as you would receive me. (1:17).
But if he has wronged you in any way or owes you anything, charge it to my account. (1:18).
I, Paul, write this with my own hand. I will repay it— not to mention that you owe me your very self. (1:19).
Yes, brother, let me have some benefit from you in the Lord. Refresh my heart in Christ. (1:20).
Confident of your obedience, I write to you, knowing that you will do even more than I ask. (1:21).
In the meantime, prepare a guest room for me, because I hope that through your prayers I will be restored to you. (1:22).
Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, sends you greetings, (1:23).
as do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow workers. (1:24).
The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. (1:25).
crossRefs: Ephesians 1:15–16: Thanksgiving for faith and love.
2 Corinthians 7:13: Comfort and joy through others’ love.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אָסִיר לַמָּשִׁיחַ (ʾāsîr la-māšîaḥ, sense), Greek: δέσμιος Χριστοῦ (désmios Christoû, NT), Aramaic: אסירא דמשיחא (ʾasirā d-mešiḥā)
translationNotes.note: Paul describes himself as imprisoned on account of his service to Christ.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul greets Philemon and gives thanks for his love, faith, and the refreshment he has brought to the saints.

intro:
Philemon is a short personal letter, only 25 verses, written by Paul during his first Roman imprisonment, likely AD 60-62. It travels alongside Colossians (notice Tychicus and Onesimus carry both, Colossians 4:7-9). Philemon was a wealthy believer in Colossae whose home hosted a church; Onesimus was his slave who had run away, found Paul somewhere, been converted, and was now returning to his master.

The letter is a masterpiece of pastoral persuasion. Paul does not command Philemon to free Onesimus, he asks. He notes Onesimus's transformation (the name means 'useful,' and Paul plays on the word: 'formerly he was useless to you, but now he is useful to you and to me'). He offers to repay any debt Onesimus owed, in his own handwriting. He drops a heavy hint that Philemon owes Paul 'your very self', meaning Philemon's own conversion came through Paul. And he asks Philemon to receive Onesimus back 'no longer as a slave but better than a slave, as a beloved brother.'

Philemon is the New Testament's quiet but decisive blow against the cultural assumption that slavery is natural. Paul does not stage a public abolition campaign; he asks one slaveholder to recognize one slave as a brother, and lets the implications travel from there. Tradition holds that Onesimus eventually became bishop of Ephesus.
